items.question:
A procurement specialist at a mid-market manufacturer has been evaluating suppliers in the same chat for over an hour — 45 turns covering pricing, quality, and logistics. His earliest messages specified that all shortlisted suppliers must offer 90-day payment terms. Claude's latest response recommends two suppliers offering only 30-day terms, with no mention of the constraint.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Claude is deliberately surfacing alternatives the specialist had not considered.
options.B: The supplier evaluation task exceeds the model's competence in commercial negotiation.
options.C: The 90-day payment terms constraint, set early in the thread, now carries less weight relative to recent content.
options.D: The most recent prompt was too vague to reference the payment terms condition.

items.question:
A copywriter at a boutique agency has been iterating on a brand voice guide in a single conversation for two days — now over 80 turns. Suggestions are growing inconsistent with tone decisions made in the first 20 turns. She needs to produce a final, coherent document.

What is the FIRST action she should take?

options.A: Ask Claude to scroll back through the full history and reproduce a complete brand voice guide from scratch.
options.B: Escalate the inconsistency to her agency's IT team for investigation.
options.C: Switch from the mid-tier to the highest-reasoning model to improve long-context retention.
options.D: Summarise the confirmed tone decisions and start a fresh chat with that summary as the opening context.

items.question:
A senior underwriter at a commercial insurer has used the same Claude conversation for three weeks to draft policy endorsement language. The thread spans hundreds of turns. He now observes that responses are shorter, miss standard clause structures present in his early templates, and occasionally contradict prior drafts.

Which factor BEST explains this quality degradation?

options.A: Accumulating context causes early critical instructions and templates to receive less attention relative to recent turns.
options.B: Claude learns from in-session feedback and gradually drifts toward patterns the underwriter most recently approved.
options.C: Claude automatically compresses old messages to manage memory, stripping out structural formatting metadata.
options.D: Very long conversations trigger a conservative output mode designed to reduce context overload risk.

items.question:
A RevOps team at a 400-person SaaS company runs 3,000 Claude API calls per day to auto-tag incoming support tickets into one of 12 categories. The logic is well-defined, responses must arrive within two seconds, and monthly costs are now a concern.

What change would MOST reduce cost without degrading task quality?

options.A: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt so Claude categorises correctly on the first attempt.
options.B: Switch from the high-reasoning tier to the fastest lightweight tier for this classification task.
options.C: Reduce the number of ticket categories from 12 to 6 to shorten the prompt.
options.D: Run the API calls in batches overnight to take advantage of off-peak pricing.

items.question:
A customer service manager at a telecoms provider has integrated Claude into a live chat tool. Agents report 8–10 second response times. Investigation reveals that every API call includes a 1,200-token copy of the full product catalogue appended to the system prompt, even when the customer's question concerns only billing.

What change would MOST reduce latency?

options.A: Shorten the system prompt by removing the agent persona description to cut token count.
options.B: Switch from the mid-tier to the lightweight model and accept slightly lower response quality.
options.C: Replace the full catalogue with only the products relevant to each query, retrieved dynamically.
options.D: Increase the maximum output token limit so Claude produces more complete answers per call.

items.question:
An internal auditor at a regional bank is trying to improve Claude's output quality on regulatory gap assessments. After a disappointing result, she simultaneously rewrites the system prompt, adds four few-shot examples, switches from the mid-tier to the highest-reasoning model, and doubles the requested output length.

What is the PRIMARY risk of making all four changes at once?

options.A: The four changes will cancel each other out, producing output identical in quality to the original.
options.B: Claude will treat simultaneous changes as conflicting instructions and refuse to process the prompt.
options.C: The cost increase from switching tiers will not be justified by the quality improvement achieved.
options.D: If quality improves, she cannot determine which change was responsible; if it worsens, she cannot isolate the cause.

items.question:
A clinical operations coordinator at a pharma company is refining a regulatory submission timeline in a long chat. Mid-conversation, she asks Claude to draft a brief project status email mentioning a "two-week contingency buffer." She then returns to timeline work. Two turns later, Claude's timeline now includes a two-week buffer not present in any prior timeline discussion, citing it as "consistent with the approach discussed earlier."

What has MOST likely occurred?

options.A: The email task injected framing that Claude is now applying to the timeline — a sign of in-thread context contamination.
options.B: Claude fabricated the buffer from pharmaceutical project norms in its training data.
options.C: The return-to-timeline prompt was ambiguous and Claude defaulted to a conservative interpretation.
options.D: Claude correctly inferred the buffer from the email and carried the decision forward as intended.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a pension fund has a rich 55-turn conversation covering a complex market scenario analysis. He now needs to ask an unrelated question: how to write a specific nested Excel formula. He worries that asking it in the existing thread could muddy the analysis context.

What is the BEST approach?

options.A: Ask the Excel question inside the existing thread, prefaced with "Ignore all prior context for this question."
options.B: Open a new chat for the unrelated question and leave the market analysis thread intact.
options.C: Formally close the market analysis conversation before opening a new one.
options.D: Add the market analysis documents to a Project so both questions can coexist in the same conversation safely.

items.question:
A bid manager at a professional services firm discovers a specific prompt structure that consistently produces excellent executive summaries for RFP responses. She uses it six times this week. The following week, she opens a new chat and cannot reconstruct the exact prompt from memory.

What practice would MOST effectively prevent this problem in future?

options.A: Maintain one long-running conversation so the successful prompt is always accessible in the history.
options.B: Ask Claude at the end of each session to reproduce the exact prompt it just executed.
options.C: Save the high-performing prompt in a shared document or as a Project instruction accessible to the team.
options.D: Note the approximate structure and rely on Claude to reconstruct the full prompt from a description of the outcome.

items.question:
A legal operations analyst uploads a 90-page vendor contract to Claude and asks it to identify all indemnification clauses. Claude returns detailed analysis of clauses in sections 1–15 and sections 22–28, but omits a clearly worded indemnification clause at section 17. The clause uses unambiguous language and is present in the uploaded file.

What is the MOST likely reason the clause was missed?

options.A: Claude's document analysis is restricted to sections explicitly named in the prompt.
options.B: The clause language is too technical for Claude's legal domain knowledge to classify reliably.
options.C: The document's formatting caused section 17 to render as a non-text image layer.
options.D: Content in the middle of a long document receives less model attention than content near the beginning or end.

items.question:
A technical writer at a software company receives a truncated API reference draft — Claude stopped mid-table after documenting 18 of 30 endpoints. She sends the follow-up message: "OK keep going."

What is the PRIMARY risk of this continuation prompt?

options.A: Without anchoring to the stopping point, Claude may repeat already-documented endpoints or skip some entirely.
options.B: Claude will interpret the casual phrasing as permission to reduce documentation quality.
options.C: The continuation will adopt a noticeably different writing style than the initial response.
options.D: Claude will ignore the instruction and restart the entire reference from endpoint 1.

items.question:
A product manager at a fintech startup is designing a pipeline that sends each user's monthly transaction summary (~600 tokens) to Claude and returns a personalised spending insight (~80 tokens). The pipeline will run for 50,000 users per month. The team debates whether to use the lightweight tier or the mid-tier model before launch.

Which factor should MOST influence the tier decision?

options.A: The mid-tier model's higher per-token cost is automatically justified by the personalisation requirement.
options.B: Whether the lightweight tier produces acceptable insight quality on a representative test sample, evaluated before scaling.
options.C: The total cost differential between tiers calculated at full volume, assessed before any quality testing.
options.D: The average response latency of each tier, given that users receive insights in their monthly app notification.

items.question:
A market researcher at a retail chain asks Claude to perform five sequential analysis steps on a dataset summary and return all five outputs in a single response. The response covers steps 1–3 fully and trails off during step 4.

What structural change to the prompting approach would MOST reliably prevent this in future?

options.A: Request only the single most critical step and discard the others.
options.B: Switch to a higher-reasoning tier model that supports longer output responses.
options.C: Request each step in a separate turn, using the prior step's output as input context for the next.
options.D: Add an explicit instruction: "Do not stop until all five steps are complete."

items.question: An HR business partner at a global bank has maintained a single Claude conversation for four months to assist with job description drafts. Recent drafts are omitting competency requirements from the firm's competency framework and adopting a more informal tone than the firm's style guide requires. Both documents were shared early in the thread. (Choose TWO factors that MOST likely explain both problems.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: The competency framework and style guide, shared early in the thread, are now far back in context and carry less weight relative to recent turns.
options.B: Claude's language model continuously updates its preferences based on user feedback expressed within a session.
options.C: Multi-month conversations trigger an automatic quality-reduction mode to manage compute.
options.D: Recent turns, including the most recent job description drafts, now dominate the model's focus, overriding earlier reference documents.
options.E: Conversational task types cause Claude to default to informal registers regardless of prior style instructions.

items.question: An engineering team at a manufacturing company is reviewing their Claude API spend, which tripled in 90 days as adoption grew. They want to cut costs without restricting usage. (Choose TWO changes that would MOST directly reduce token cost without degrading output quality for well-defined tasks.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Ask Claude to explain its reasoning in every response to improve accuracy and reduce costly retries.
options.B: Remove boilerplate from system prompts that repeats on every API call but adds no task-relevant instruction.
options.C: Use the lightweight model tier for high-volume routine tasks that do not require deep reasoning.
options.D: Increase the maximum output token limit so Claude produces longer, more complete responses and reduces re-runs.
options.E: Move all tasks to asynchronous batch processing regardless of whether the use case requires real-time responses.

items.question: A strategy consultant at a 90,000-person professional services firm is completing a two-week engagement. She has used a single Claude conversation throughout — 120+ turns covering market sizing, competitor profiles, and risk assessment. She must now write the executive summary, the highest-stakes output of the engagement. (Choose TWO actions that would MOST improve the executive summary's quality.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Distil the key findings, decisions, and constraints from the full thread into a concise briefing document before writing.
options.B: Ask Claude to review all 120 turns and produce a self-summary, then use that as context for the executive summary.
options.C: Start a fresh conversation using the briefing document as the sole context for the executive summary task.
options.D: Switch to a higher-reasoning model tier while remaining in the same 120-turn thread to boost quality.
options.E: Tag the ten most important turns in the conversation so Claude weights them more heavily in the summary.

items.question: A legal analyst at an insurance company asks Claude to draft a 15-clause exclusions schedule for a new product policy. The response covers clauses 1–9 and stops. The analyst needs all 15 clauses in consistent numbering format and style. (Choose TWO approaches that would MOST reliably produce the remaining clauses in matching style.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Start a new chat and request all 15 clauses again from scratch, emphasising consistency.
options.B: In the same chat, ask: "Please draft clauses 10–15, maintaining the same numbering format and clause style as clauses 1–9 above."
options.C: Ask Claude to regenerate clauses 1–9 in a shorter format to create room for all remaining clauses in one response.
options.D: Upload the partial draft as a new file attachment and request completion in a fresh chat session.
options.E: Paste clauses 8 and 9 as style anchors in the follow-up prompt, then request clauses 10–15 explicitly.

items.question:
A compliance manager at a fintech firm has used a single Claude conversation for 75 turns to draft policy sections. Quality was strong in turns 1–30. Since turn 50, responses have been missing mandatory regulatory references that were included in her early instructions, and formatting has become inconsistent. She is about to intervene.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Upgrade to the highest-reasoning model tier to compensate for the quality decline in the long thread.
options.B: Delete the last 20 turns from the conversation history to restore the earlier context weighting.
options.C: Extract the key instructions, regulatory references, and completed decisions into a summary document, then open a fresh conversation with that summary as the opening context.
options.D: Repeat the regulatory references verbatim at the start of each new prompt for the remaining policy sections.

items.question:
A learning and development manager at a university is drafting a course module on sensitive workplace topics. Claude's response ends mid-sentence with no closing remark after covering two of five planned sections. She wonders whether Claude refused to continue because the content was sensitive.

What is the MOST reliable way to distinguish output truncation from a refusal?

options.A: Truncation ends mid-sentence with no explanation; refusal includes an explicit statement declining to continue.
options.B: Truncation occurs only on sensitive topics; refusal occurs when the model hits its output length limit.
options.C: Refusal produces shorter output than truncation; truncation always includes a closing phrase.
options.D: Both produce identical output signatures; the difference requires testing on a different model tier to confirm.

items.question:
An account executive at a financial services firm has a Claude Project with the instruction: "All outreach emails must be formal and concise." A key client has specifically requested a warm, casual follow-up. The AE asks Claude in the chat: "Write a casual, friendly follow-up email for this client." Claude produces a polished but noticeably formal email.

What does this MOST likely indicate?

options.A: Claude is incapable of producing informal output — the formal constraint is a platform-level restriction.
options.B: The Project-level instruction for formal tone is overriding the per-chat request; the chat prompt must explicitly suspend or override it for this task.
options.C: Claude detected a brand risk in writing casually on behalf of a regulated firm and defaulted to the safer register.
options.D: The chat prompt was too vague about the desired level of informality for Claude to act on it.

items.question:
An operations manager at an energy company pastes 48 hours of equipment sensor readings into a Claude prompt and asks for predicted failure rates for the next week. Claude produces confident-sounding numerical predictions. His engineering team reviews them and determines they are statistically unreliable — not grounded in the firm's historical failure distributions or validated modelling methodology.

Which assessment MOST accurately describes the situation?

options.A: This is a prompt problem — including more sensor data history would produce reliable predictions.
options.B: This is a model tier problem — the highest-reasoning tier would produce statistically sound predictions.
options.C: Predictive failure-rate modelling requires statistical methodology and domain calibration that Claude is not designed to provide; this task is a poor fit for autonomous output.
options.D: This is a context problem — Claude needs baseline historical failure rate distributions to calibrate its predictions.

items.question:
A data scientist at a pharma company uses Claude via the API. He notices that short requests complete fully, but requests expected to produce more than 2,000 tokens always truncate at approximately the same position. He has tried five different prompt phrasings. The pattern is perfectly consistent.

What should he do FIRST before escalating to IT?

options.A: Switch to the enterprise subscription tier to unlock longer output responses.
options.B: Test the same long prompts in Claude.ai to determine whether the issue is API-specific.
options.C: File a support ticket with Anthropic describing the observed truncation behaviour.
options.D: Check whether the API call code specifies a max_tokens parameter that is capping output at the observed threshold.

items.question:
A content strategist at a media company has been drafting advertising copy in a long conversation. In her first turn, she included a detailed brief requiring mandatory disclosure language on all ad copy. Recent drafts omit the disclosures entirely. She wonders whether Claude lacks knowledge of the applicable advertising standards.

Which explanation MOST likely accounts for the omission?

options.A: The disclosure requirement, established early in a long thread, is being diluted by more recent content — this is conversation drift.
options.B: Claude lacks training data on the specific advertising standards applicable to this media format.
options.C: Claude is optimising output length by omitting elements it considers standard boilerplate.
options.D: The disclosure requirement was too detailed to carry across multiple turns without re-statement.

items.question:
A product designer at a retail tech startup has integrated Claude into a product description generator. Average response time is 12 seconds. Prompts average 400 tokens; responses average 600 tokens. The engineering lead suggests reducing the maximum output token limit to cut latency.

What should the team verify FIRST before adjusting the output limit?

options.A: Whether the lightweight model tier would produce acceptable descriptions with meaningfully lower latency.
options.B: Whether the 12-second latency is driven primarily by input processing or output generation, since reducing the output limit only addresses the output-generation portion of the delay.
options.C: Whether the product brief can be shortened to under 200 tokens without degrading description quality.
options.D: Whether the API rate limit is being hit and causing queuing delays that account for most of the 12 seconds.

items.question:
A risk analyst at an insurance company is 30 turns into a conversation analysing a reinsurance treaty — with specific treaty terms, carve-outs, and constraints established in the first 15 turns. A colleague asks her to analyse a completely separate reinsurance treaty for a different client. She considers whether to continue in the same conversation.

What is the BEST approach?

options.A: Continue in the same conversation to benefit from the shared reinsurance structure knowledge established in earlier turns.
options.B: Add a clear separator message in the chat and continue in the same thread.
options.C: Start a new conversation for the second treaty to prevent the first treaty's specific terms from contaminating the analysis.
options.D: Archive the first conversation and then start a new one from the same Project.

items.question:
A communications director at a non-profit has a Project instruction: "Maintain a formal, institutional tone in all communications." She asks Claude in a chat: "Write a casual fundraising Instagram post that feels personal and warm." Claude's output is slightly warmer than usual but still noticeably formal. She adjusts the chat prompt three more times. Each iteration remains formal.

What does this MOST likely indicate?

options.A: Claude cannot produce casual content — the formal tone instruction is a hard platform constraint.
options.B: Claude has inferred that an Instagram post for a non-profit would damage brand credibility if too casual.
options.C: The chat prompts still lack sufficient specificity about what "personal and warm" means in this context.
options.D: The Project-level instruction is dominating; the Project instruction must be explicitly suspended for this task to allow the casual register.

items.question:
A finance director at a 90,000-person logistics company is reviewing three proposed approaches to reduce Claude API costs: (1) route all tasks to the cheapest model tier regardless of task type; (2) route tasks to the appropriate tier based on their complexity — cheapest for routine work, higher tiers for complex analysis; (3) improve prompts on all tasks to reduce retry rates.

Which option represents the MOST principled approach?

options.A: Option 2 — match tier to task complexity, preserving quality on high-stakes work while reducing cost on routine volume.
options.B: Option 1 — apply the cheapest tier universally to achieve the maximum unit cost reduction across all tasks.
options.C: Option 3 — improve prompts first, since better prompts reduce retries and therefore total API cost.
options.D: Defer all three options until the team produces a full cost-by-task breakdown.

items.question:
An actuarial analyst at a life insurance company uploads a 60-page methodology document and asks Claude to flag deviations from the firm's actuarial standards. She notices that deviations in sections 1–20 and 40–60 are consistently identified, but deviations in sections 20–35 are frequently missed.

What is the MOST effective mitigation for this specific pattern?

options.A: Upgrade to the highest-reasoning model tier to improve mid-document attention.
options.B: Send a targeted follow-up prompt asking Claude to review sections 20–35 specifically for methodology deviations.
options.C: Split the document at section 20 and upload two separate files for separate analysis runs.
options.D: Add an explicit instruction: "Pay special attention to sections 20–35, which are the most critical."

items.question:
A digital transformation lead at a public sector agency uploads a 12,000-word policy brief and asks for a structured gap analysis. The response is generic, misses specific policy sections he referenced by name, and ignores the output format he specified. He has rephrased the prompt twice. Same result.

Before escalating to IT, what should he verify FIRST?

options.A: That the file type is supported for upload in the current interface version.
options.B: That the same prompt in a fresh conversation, without the prior rephrasing history, produces the same result.
options.C: That the file is rendering as parseable text, by testing a simple targeted question about a specific named section of the document.
options.D: That the enterprise subscription tier includes document analysis for files of this length.

items.question:
A supply chain coordinator at an automotive manufacturer has refined a Claude prompt for supplier risk summaries over three weeks. It now produces excellent output. He wants to adapt it for customer credit risk summaries — a related but different use case — and plans to simultaneously change the role description, the output format, and the evaluation criteria.

What is the PRIMARY reason to make these changes one at a time instead?

options.A: Claude will interpret three simultaneous instruction changes as conflicting and fail to apply any of them.
options.B: Changing the format and criteria together will create a prompt that exceeds the context limit for this use case.
options.C: The original supplier risk prompt will be permanently altered and unrecoverable after simultaneous changes.
options.D: If the adapted prompt underperforms, he cannot determine whether the role, format, or criteria change caused the problem — or identify which element to revert.

items.question:
A medical writer at a biotech startup is asked whether Claude could automatically generate the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) for an upcoming Phase III clinical trial. The SAP must be pre-specified before data unblinding, signed by the principal investigator, and auditable by regulators.

What is the MOST significant reason this task is a poor fit for autonomous Claude output?

options.A: Claude lacks sufficient training data on Phase III clinical trial designs to produce an accurate SAP.
options.B: The SAP format is too highly structured for Claude to follow without significant prompt engineering.
options.C: The cost of using Claude for a document of this length and complexity would exceed the benefit.
options.D: An SAP requires expert statistical judgment, regulatory pre-specification, and accountable sign-off by a qualified investigator — none of which Claude can provide.

items.question:
An internal communications manager at a 400-store retail chain has used a prompt template for monthly all-hands briefing summaries for 18 months. A new executive team has requested a different tone and structure. She must decide whether to modify the existing template incrementally or rebuild from scratch.

What approach would MOST efficiently reach a high-quality new template?

options.A: Rebuild from scratch to avoid carrying over assumptions embedded in the old template.
options.B: Modify the existing template incrementally, one element at a time, testing quality after each change.
options.C: Ask Claude to redesign the template itself based on a description of the new executive team's preferences.
options.D: Run the old and new templates in parallel for one month to empirically compare output quality before committing.

items.question:
A grant writer at a research university has maintained a single Claude conversation for six weeks to draft a multi-year funding application. His turn-3 instruction: "Use numbered lists for all supporting evidence." Section 5 (drafted in turn 20) and section 12 (drafted in turn 60) both ignore this formatting constraint. He wants to determine whether the problem is conversation drift or an ambiguous original instruction.

Which finding would MOST conclusively indicate conversation drift rather than an ambiguous constraint?

options.A: Section 5, drafted in turn 20, also ignores the constraint — suggesting it was never understood from the start.
options.B: The numbered-list instruction appears only in the chat turn and not in the Project instructions.
options.C: Sections drafted in turns 1–15 correctly use numbered lists; sections after turn 40 progressively drop them.
options.D: The constraint was phrased as "use numbered lists" rather than the more explicit "format all supporting evidence as numbered lists."

items.question: A marketing team lead at a hospitality company has set up a Claude Project with instructions for formal tone, brand colour guidance, and a prohibition on competitor mentions. Team members report that per-chat requests to use a lighter tone or reference a competitor's pricing are routinely overridden by the Project instructions. (Choose TWO statements that MOST accurately describe this behaviour and its correct resolution.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Project-level instructions take precedence over individual chat prompts by default — this is expected, by-design behaviour.
options.B: Project instructions should be deleted and recreated as per-chat instructions for each task to give users more flexibility.
options.C: For tasks requiring a legitimate deviation, the chat prompt must explicitly state the exception or override for that specific task.
options.D: Claude will always apply the more restrictive of the two competing instructions regardless of context.
options.E: Consistent override of chat-level requests by Project instructions indicates a configuration error that IT should investigate.

items.question: An operations analyst at a telecoms provider experiences two API problems: (A) identical prompts produce good output on some runs and mediocre output on others; (B) responses consistently fail to follow a JSON output format specified in the system prompt, despite multiple rephrasing attempts. She considers escalating both to IT. (Choose TWO statements that are TRUE about each problem and the appropriate response.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Problem A (run-to-run inconsistency) indicates a server-side model defect that IT support can resolve by adjusting inference parameters.
options.B: Problem A (run-to-run inconsistency) is expected probabilistic behaviour; it is managed through prompt engineering or temperature settings, not escalation.
options.C: Problem B (JSON format failure) is always a model capability limitation; it should be escalated without further prompt work.
options.D: Problem B (JSON format failure) warrants deeper prompt engineering — explicit schema examples, structured output instructions — before IT escalation, since format failures are most commonly prompt specification issues.
options.E: Both problems should be escalated together so IT has full context for a combined diagnosis.

items.question: A compliance officer at an investment management firm is evaluating two proposed uses of Claude: Task 1 — reviewing client suitability assessments and making approve/reject recommendations; Task 2 — drafting the compliance team's internal written commentary on each assessment for the file record. (Choose TWO statements that correctly identify the appropriate fit boundary.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Task 1 is a poor fit for autonomous Claude output because it is a consequential financial decision requiring accountable human judgment and regulatory defensibility.
options.B: Task 1 is appropriate for Claude because suitability criteria are defined rules that Claude can apply consistently and efficiently.
options.C: Task 2 is a poor fit because internal commentary on client assessments contains sensitive financial data.
options.D: Task 2 is a poor fit because Claude cannot draft commentary without direct human input on each individual case.
options.E: Task 2 is appropriate for Claude to support by drafting internal commentary for human review, reducing analyst effort without displacing the human decision-maker.

items.question: A legal counsel at a manufacturing company is mid-conversation in a 30-turn analysis of a licensing agreement. A colleague requests help with an unrelated contract dispute. He considers whether to handle the dispute in the same conversation. (Choose TWO factors that MOST strongly support starting a new conversation for the dispute.) (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude cannot maintain two separate legal analyses simultaneously in the same context window.
options.B: The licensing agreement's specific terms and constraints would be present in the context, risking their influence on the unrelated dispute analysis.
options.C: A fresh conversation ensures the dispute analysis is not coloured by framing introduced during the licensing agreement work.
options.D: Switching topics within a conversation causes Claude to reduce output quality on subsequent tasks.
options.E: The licensing agreement conversation will be automatically archived once a new topic is introduced.

items.question:
A digital product manager at a fintech startup is testing a new Claude API integration. Short queries complete fully and correctly. However, queries expected to produce more than approximately 1,500 tokens of output always truncate at the same position — regardless of prompt content, phrasing, or model tier. He has reproduced the pattern five times.

What should he do NEXT?

options.A: Inspect the API call code to check whether a max_tokens parameter is set to a value that matches the observed truncation threshold.
options.B: Switch to the highest-reasoning model tier, which supports longer per-response output.
options.C: File a support ticket with Anthropic immediately — consistent truncation at a fixed position indicates a platform-level defect.
options.D: Restructure all queries to produce outputs under 1,500 tokens to avoid the threshold entirely.

items.question:
A senior editor at a publishing house asks Claude for a 20-item editorial checklist. She receives items 1–12 and truncation. She sends: "Please continue with the remaining items." The follow-up response includes 3 items that overlap substantially with items already in the first 12.

What addition to the continuation prompt would MOST reliably prevent duplication?

options.A: Specify the exact starting number: "Continue from item 13, completing items 13 through 20."
options.B: Start a new conversation and request all 20 items with an explicit instruction to avoid repetition.
options.C: Ask Claude to regenerate all 20 items in a single response to ensure internal consistency.
options.D: Ask Claude to review items 1–12 again before continuing, so it knows what has already been covered.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a government ministry has been drafting a regulatory impact assessment across a 40-turn conversation. She notices in turn 38 that Claude has been using slightly different definitions for "SME" and "regulated entity" than the official definitions she included in turn 2. The drafts are internally consistent but diverge subtly from the official terms of reference.

This pattern is MOST accurately characterised as:

options.A: A knowledge gap — Claude does not have reliable access to this government's official definitions.
options.B: Conversation drift causing subtle definitional substitution that is internally coherent but diverges from the original source instruction.
options.C: A prompt vagueness issue — the original definitions in turn 2 were not expressed with sufficient precision.
options.D: Acceptable variation — minor definitional drift is within normal operating parameters for extended drafting work.

items.question:
An HR technology manager at a global enterprise is generating implementation documentation for a new HR system — 30 sections in a single long conversation. After multiple continuation prompts, sections 1–18 are complete and consistent. From section 19 onward, the content begins losing consistency with prior sections and repeating guidance already covered in sections 5 and 12. The thread is now very long.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Send a continuation prompt listing all guidance that must not be repeated in the remaining sections.
options.B: Add a summary table of completed sections to the next prompt and continue in the same thread.
options.C: Compile sections 1–18 into a structured summary, start a fresh conversation, and complete sections 19–30 with that summary as context.
options.D: Switch to the highest-reasoning tier to improve cross-section consistency in very long threads.

items.question:
A mid-market accounting firm recently switched all Claude API tasks to the lightweight tier, reducing monthly costs by 60%. The tax team now reports that first-draft tax research summaries are missing case law references and producing shallow analysis. Partners are raising quality concerns.

What is the MOST appropriate corrective action?

options.A: Revert all tasks back to the highest-reasoning tier to fully restore quality across the board.
options.B: Add more detailed prompts to compensate for the lightweight tier's depth limitations on complex analysis.
options.C: Accept the quality reduction and address partner complaints by improving human review processes.
options.D: Return complex tax research analysis tasks to a higher tier while keeping simpler, well-defined tasks on the lightweight tier.

items.question:
A contract specialist at a construction company must review a 120-page infrastructure contract for obligation and liability clauses. She is deciding between uploading the full document for a single comprehensive review and splitting it into three 40-page sections reviewed separately.

Which factor MOST supports choosing the sectional approach over the full-document upload?

options.A: Clauses in the middle 40 pages may receive less model attention than those near the start and end of the full document.
options.B: Full document uploads take significantly longer to process and may time out before the review completes.
options.C: A 120-page document is likely to exceed Claude's maximum supported document size for analysis.
options.D: Claude cannot cross-reference obligation clauses across pages when reviewing a full document at once.

items.question:
A brand manager at a large FMCG company has a 50-turn Claude conversation developing a comprehensive brand refresh strategy. She is observing drift in the latest outputs. Before starting a fresh conversation, she must decide what to capture from the existing thread.

What is the PRIMARY information she must document before starting fresh?

options.A: The date and time of each significant turn, to reconstruct the decision timeline if needed.
options.B: The settled strategic decisions, brand principles, and constraints agreed upon throughout the thread.
options.C: The exact wording of Claude's best responses, to be reused verbatim in the new conversation.
options.D: Her original brief from turn 1, which can serve as the complete context for the new conversation.

items.question:
An operations manager at a pharmaceutical manufacturer has spent two weeks trying to extract structured data from batch manufacturing records using Claude. He has tested five prompt variations, added explicit few-shot examples, specified the output schema, and tested on multiple record types. Every attempt produces systematic errors in the same three fields. The documents are confirmed as text-parseable.

What is the MOST appropriate next action?

options.A: Try a different few-shot example strategy before escalating.
options.B: Accept that the three problematic fields cannot be extracted reliably and adjust the downstream workflow.
options.C: Escalate to IT or technical support, providing the prompt, sample records, and documented failure pattern for investigation.
options.D: Switch to the highest-reasoning tier, which has stronger structured extraction capability.

items.question:
An investment analyst at an asset management firm has been iterating on a prompt for comparable company analysis for four weeks. Versions 2–4 improved incrementally over the failing version 1. Version 5 was the best result yet. Version 8, the latest, performs worse than version 5. Each iteration has added instructions to address gaps revealed by the prior version.

What does this trajectory MOST likely indicate, and what should he do?

options.A: He has reached the model's reasoning ceiling for this analysis type; he should switch to the highest-reasoning tier.
options.B: The recent additions have introduced conflicting instructions; he should remove the last three additions and test version 5 again.
options.C: Version 8 outperformed version 5 on dimensions he has not measured; he needs a more comprehensive evaluation rubric before reverting.
options.D: The prompt has become overloaded by cumulative additions; he should return to version 5 as his known baseline and make only one targeted change from there.

items.question:
A university library has set up a Claude Project with 12 custom instructions covering tone, citation formats, response length, audience calibration, five terminology restrictions, and subject boundaries. Library staff report that Claude frequently produces incomplete or hedged responses on simple reference queries, as if unable to proceed.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Overspecified Project instructions contain conflicting constraints that Claude cannot simultaneously satisfy.
options.B: Claude requires all custom instructions to be written in a priority order to resolve conflicts between them.
options.C: The 12 instructions exceed the maximum number of custom instructions allowed per Project.
options.D: Library staff are submitting requests outside the subject boundaries specified in the instructions.

items.question:
A logistics planner at a freight company currently uses Claude to draft delay communications — a writing task that is clearly appropriate. Operations leadership now proposes extending Claude's role to generate recommended rerouting plans for delayed shipments, based on current route data and availability matrices the planner would paste in.

What factor would MOST determine whether this extended use is appropriate?

options.A: Whether the company has an enterprise subscription with higher API throughput for operational tasks.
options.B: Whether a qualified logistics expert reviews Claude's recommendations before they are acted upon.
options.C: Whether the model tier selected has sufficient capacity for logistics optimisation complexity.
options.D: Whether Claude's training data covers freight routing patterns similar to this company's network.

items.question:
A clinical trial manager at a medical device company is building a workflow where Claude reviews incoming adverse event reports and flags potential device-related events. To reduce latency, the engineering team proposes caching the system prompt, which contains the device's current contraindication list. The list is updated approximately once per quarter by the safety team.

What is the PRIMARY risk of this caching strategy?

options.A: Cached prompts increase per-token cost compared to uncached prompts of the same length.
options.B: Prompt caching creates a dependency on network connectivity that could cause unpredictable system downtime.
options.C: If the contraindication list is updated between cache refreshes, Claude will screen adverse events against an outdated list until the cache is explicitly reset.
options.D: Cached system prompts prevent Claude from adapting to new adverse event terminology introduced in recent reports.

items.question:
A treasury analyst at an energy company has maintained a single Claude conversation for five months to develop cash flow models across multiple scenarios. He has never documented the governing assumptions, formulas, or model constraints outside the conversation. The thread is now hundreds of turns long and output quality has severely degraded. He now decides to start fresh.

What is the MOST significant consequence of waiting this long?

options.A: The conversation history will be permanently deleted when he opens a new chat.
options.B: Five months of context drift may have introduced errors into his output documents that now require a full accuracy review.
options.C: The new conversation will not have access to the same model version that was available when the original conversation started.
options.D: The governing assumptions and model logic were never captured externally, so he cannot provide adequate context for the fresh start.
